![](figs/manor_house.png){fig-alt="Miss Marple examines a will at a manor-house desk as the maid, butler, and three relatives look on. An amber poison bottle stands nearby."}

Lutz (2026), "Statistical sleuths versus AI: Unmasking the killer in Agatha Christie
novels", *Significance* 23(6), 10–15, coded 166 main characters in the 12 Miss Marple
novels (14 killers) by gender, employment, relation to the victim, and financial gain, and
added three AI "guesses" (Harvard AI Sandbox, GPT 5.1/5.6) based on the opening of each
novel. This document reproduces her analysis, corrects the odds ratios in her Table 1, and
extends it with multivariable and conditional (within-novel) logistic models.
Only the code for the key models is shown here. All of the code, including the figures,
is in `AgathaChristie.R`.

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| code-fold: true
#| results: hold
```

## The data

Lutz's data, from her [GitHub repository](https://github.com/SharonLutz/Stats-vs-AI-whodunnit),
have one row per character, with the novel's title and 0/1 indicators for being the
killer, the four character traits, and the three AI guesses. The setup code above reads
them and makes No/Yes factor copies for tables and plots.

The output below gives the counts, the percentage of characters with each trait (or
flagged by each AI guess), and a three-way table of Killer by Related and Financial gain,
the two traits that matter most. The last two lines test the association between Related
and Financial gain.

```{r}
#| label: describe
#| code-fold: true
#| results: hold
```

Only 8.4% of the characters are killers, 14 in 12 novels (two novels have two). About
half the characters are female and most are employed, but only 16% are related to the
victim and 10% stand to gain financially. Each AI guess flags 10–14% of the characters.

The table already tells most of the story. Of the 14 characters who are both related and
stand to gain, 8 are killers, while only 2 of the 137 with neither trait are. Related and
Financial gain also go together (OR = 53): an heir is usually a relative. Lutz's
chi-square of 58.3 for this table is the Yates-corrected value (uncorrected, 63.8). With
expected counts this small, the odds ratio is the better summary.

## Reproducing Lutz's Table 1

Lutz's Table 1 gives, for each predictor on its own, an odds ratio with its confidence
interval and *p*-value, and the AUC. Her multivariable models are reported only by their
AUCs. The first step is to see whether these numbers can be reproduced, and how they
were calculated.

### Univariate "odds ratios"

Lutz's odds ratios are all between 0.98 and 1.75, which is far too small for binary
predictors with AUCs of 0.80 or more. They are reproduced *exactly* by exponentiating the
slopes of a **linear probability model** (`glm(..., family = gaussian)`), i.e. exp(difference
in proportions), not by logistic regression:

```{r}
#| label: lutz-table1
```

A difference in proportions lies between −1 and 1, so its exponential can never be
smaller than 1/e ≈ 0.37 or larger than e ≈ 2.72, however strong the association. Her AUCs
are not affected: with a single binary predictor, every model ranks the characters the
same way. Her *p*-values, also from the linear model, are much smaller than the logistic
ones below, but they put the predictors in the same order. It is the odds ratios
themselves that are wrong.

### Multivariable AUCs

The AUC (area under the ROC curve) is the probability that a randomly chosen killer gets a
higher fitted score than a randomly chosen innocent character: 0.5 is chance, 1 is
perfect. Her four multivariable models add each AI guess, in turn, to Related and
Financial gain. Fitting them as logistic regressions, her AUCs (0.89, 0.89, 0.97, 0.92)
reproduce too:

```{r}
#| label: lutz-multi
#| code-fold: true
#| results: hold
```

So the problem is confined to the odds ratios. Adding the AI's web-based guess raises the
AUC from 0.89 to 0.97; the other two guesses add little.

## Correct odds ratios

For a binary outcome, the odds ratio comes from logistic regression: exp(slope) in
`glm(Killer ~ x, family = binomial)` is the odds of being the killer for characters with
the trait, divided by the odds for those without it. For a single binary predictor this
is just the cross-product ratio of the 2 × 2 table.

### Univariate logistic regressions

The code fits one logistic regression for each predictor, with profile-likelihood 95%
confidence intervals, and sets the result beside Lutz's values (`Lutz_OR`). The rows are
sorted by AUC, so the weakest predictors come first.

```{r}
#| label: uni-logit
```

The correct odds ratios are much larger than Lutz's. A character who gains financially from
the murder has about 50 times the odds of being the killer; being related to the victim,
about 20 times. Gender and employment are irrelevant. The AI guesses fall in between,
with odds ratios of 6 to 19. The AUCs are unchanged, because AUC depends only on how the
fitted values rank the characters, and with one binary predictor every model ranks them the
same way.

The confidence intervals are wide (financial gain: 14 to 233), as they must be with only 14
killers. The odds ratios are clearly different from 1, but their size is not well
determined.

### Fourfold displays

A fourfold display shows each 2 × 2 table as four quarter circles, one per cell, with
area proportional to the cell count. Here the counts are first standardized so that both
margins are equal. This removes the fact that only 8% of the characters are killers,
leaving only the association.

In each panel below, the rows are Killer (No at top, Yes at bottom) and the columns are
the predictor (No at left, Yes at right). The raw counts are in the corners. When the
odds ratio is greater than 1, the No/No and Yes/Yes quadrants (top left and bottom right)
are larger than the other two, and the white diagonal runs between them. The rings around
each quadrant show 95% confidence limits for the odds ratio: if the rings for adjacent
quadrants don't overlap, the odds ratio differs significantly from 1, and those panels
are shaded in darker colors.

```{r}
#| label: fig-fourfold
#| code-fold: true
#| results: hold
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-cap: "Fourfold displays (ggfourfold) of Killer (top/bottom) by each predictor (left/right). Quarter-circle areas show the cell frequencies, standardized to equal margins; non-overlapping 95% confidence rings and intense shading mean the odds ratio differs from 1. The white diagonal marks the direction of association."
```

The panels for Female and Employed are nearly round, with overlapping rings and pale
shading: no association. In the other five, the Yes/Yes quadrant of killers with the trait
is far larger than its neighbors, most of all for Related and Financial gain. The AI
guesses look much like the character traits, but weaker, and the ~20% passage is the
weakest of all.

## All non-AI predictors together

The univariate odds ratios ask about each predictor on its own, but Related and Financial
are strongly associated (OR ≈ 53), so they partly tell the same story. To see what each
contributes *given the others*, fit one logistic model with all four non-AI predictors.
`drop1()` gives a likelihood-ratio (LR) test for removing each term from the full model.
LR tests are more trustworthy than the Wald *z* tests in `summary()` when there are only
14 events.

### Main-effects model

```{r}
#| label: full-logit
```

With all four together, financial gain carries most of the weight (LR χ² = 12.9,
p < .001). Related is only marginal once gain is in the model (p = .10), and Female adds
nothing.

### Effect plot

An effect plot shows the same model on the probability scale. Each panel gives the fitted
probability of being the killer at each level of one predictor, averaging over the other
three, with 95% confidence intervals.

```{r}
#| label: fig-effects
#| code-fold: true
#| results: hold
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-cap: "Effect plot for the four-predictor logistic model: fitted probability of being the killer at each level of one predictor, averaged over the others, with 95% confidence intervals. The y-axis is on the logit scale, which is common to all panels; the dashed line is the overall proportion of killers (14/166)."
```

Financial gain moves the probability of guilt from about 2% to 40%, and being related
moves it from 2% to 13%. Employed now looks positive (adjusted OR ≈ 4.6, against 1.1 on
its own), but its interval is wide (p = .16). The shift happens because employed
characters rarely gain financially (7 of 103), but 6 of those 7 are killers.

### Related × Financial interaction

Is the effect of financial gain the same for relatives and non-relatives? Adding a
Related × Financial interaction tests this:

```{r}
#| label: full-interaction
```

The interaction is significant (p = .02). With only 3 unrelated characters who gained
financially, 2 of them killers, financial gain matters even more for the unrelated. The
mosaic display in @fig-mosaic shows this.

```{r}
#| label: fig-mosaic
#| code-fold: true
#| results: hold
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-cap: "Mosaic display of Killer by Related and Financial gain, shaded by residuals from the model in which Killer is independent of the two predictors. 8 of the 14 related characters with something to gain are killers."
```

### Reducing the model and adding the AI guesses

Finally, two questions about the predictor set. Can Female and Employed be dropped
together, leaving Related + Financial as the base model? And once Related and Financial
are known, does each AI guess add anything? Both are LR tests of nested models.

```{r}
#| label: ai-add
#| code-fold: true
#| results: hold
```

Female and Employed together add nothing (p = 0.14), so Related + Financial is the base
model from here on. Adding the AI's web-based Chapter 1 guess improves it a lot (LR
χ² = 16.5, AUC 0.97), and adding the pasted Chapter 1 helps less (p = .01). The ~20%
passage adds nothing significant (p = .14).

## Conditional logistic regression: comparing suspects within a novel

Each novel is a closed circle of suspects with one (or two) killers, so the natural model
compares the killer with the other characters *in the same book*: conditional logit with
`strata(Title)`, e.g.

```r
clogit(Killer ~ Female + Employed + Related + Financial + strata(Title), data = dat)
```

The output below shows, for each novel, the number of characters and killers and how many
gain financially. It then gives univariate conditional ORs, LR tests for dropping each term
from the full model, and LR tests for adding each AI guess to Related + Financial.

```{r}
#| label: clogit
#| code-fold: true
#| results: hold
```

The striking result is that **financial gain is perfectly separated within novels**: in
every novel where any innocent character gains financially, the killer does too. Its
conditional odds ratio is infinite, so we report likelihood-ratio tests rather than Wald
tests. Within novels, Related and Financial remain strong; of the AI guesses, only the one
that "read" Chapter 1 from the web adds anything once Related and Financial are known.

The conditional odds ratios for the other predictors (column `OR`) are close to the
ordinary ones (`glm_OR`), except for Related, which rises from 21 to 69. Comparing
suspects within a book sharpens the effect of being related to the victim.

## Whom would Miss Marple accuse?

AUC pools all 166 characters, but the reader's real question is "which of *these*
suspects did it?" Here each novel's top-scoring suspect(s) are accused, and we record the
chance of accusing the right one (averaged over the 12 novels).

The scores are the linear predictors from the conditional logit models, or the 0/1 values
themselves for a single predictor. With binary predictors, several suspects often tie for
the top score. Miss Marple then picks one of them at random, so a novel scores the
proportion of killers among its top-ranked suspects. "Chance" means accusing any
character in the novel at random.

```{r}
#| label: accuse
#| code-fold: true
#| results: hold
```

Guessing at random is right 8% of the time. Following the money alone is right 57% of the
time, Related + Financial 68%, and adding the AI's web-based Chapter 1 guess, 85%.

## Leave-one-novel-out cross-validation

All of the above is in-sample: 14 killers, and models chosen after looking at the data.
To mimic predicting the killer in a novel you haven't read, each model is fit to 11
novels and used to score the characters of the 12th, for each novel in turn.

In the output, `AUC_in` and `AUC_cv` are the in-sample and cross-validated AUCs from the
logistic models. The `hit_` columns are the accusation hit rates of the previous section,
in-sample and cross-validated, for the logistic (`glm`) and conditional logit (`cl`)
models. When a CV value is close to the in-sample one, the model is not just fitting
the noise in these 166 characters.

```{r}
#| label: cv
#| code-fold: true
#| results: hold
```

Scores use the fitted slopes only. A held-out novel's killer is missing from training
exactly when it matters, which lowers that fold's intercept, and pooling scores across
folds then biases the CV AUC downward. With intercepts included, the single-AI-predictor
CV AUCs fall to 0.51–0.64, an artifact of pooling, not a real loss of
discrimination. Within-novel rankings (hit rates) are unaffected either way.

* **Related + Financial + AI web holds up**: CV AUC 0.94 (in-sample 0.97), and the
  best CV hit rate (76%).
* **Female and Employed are overfitting**: adding them raises in-sample AUC (0.91) but
  *lowers* CV AUC (0.83 vs. 0.88 for Related + Financial alone), and the CV hit rate falls
  to 55–63%.
* Related + Financial alone is the most stable model: 68% hit rate in-sample and in CV.

### Doubledecker plots: where the AI guess helps

Where does the AI's web-based guess add to Related and Financial gain? A doubledecker plot
divides the characters into a bar for each combination of the predictors, with width
proportional to the number of characters. The height of the red part of each bar is the
proportion of killers in that group.

```{r}
#| label: fig-doubledecker
#| code-fold: true
#| results: hold
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-cap: "Doubledecker plots: the proportion of killers (red) in each combination of Related, Gain and the AI's guess."
#| fig-subcap:
#|   - "AI guess from Chapter 1 on the web"
#|   - "AI guess from Chapter 1 pasted in"
#| layout-ncol: 1
```

The two plots differ in one group: the 137 characters who are neither related nor stand to
gain, the wide bars at the left. Two killers hide among them, with no obvious motive. The
web-based guess flags 14 of these characters, and both killers are among them; no killer
is among the 123 it leaves out. The guess from the pasted Chapter 1 flags 9 of them, and
misses both killers. Among related characters with something to gain, both guesses do
about equally well (4 of 5 flagged are killers, against 4 of 9 not flagged).

Finding the killers that motive can't find is exactly what an AI that remembers how the
book ends would do. This is the leakage concern in the caveats below.

## Caveats

* 14 killers in 12 novels: models with more than two or three predictors overfit, and
  in-sample AUCs and hit rates are optimistic (see the cross-validation above). With 12
  folds, the CV estimates themselves are noisy.
* Lutz notes that the "web" AI condition performed better than giving the AI the same text
  directly, which suggests it was drawing on outside knowledge of these famous books. Its
  advantage may be partly leakage, not reading.
